column2: At this point the Seventh Lady came to call them to supper. The Gu household was decidedly Western in style. A long mahogany dining table stood in the middle of the room, surrounded by six chairs in the French court style. The seating, however, followed Chinese custom: the places at the ends of the table were treated as seats of honour. Gu and his wife sat to either side of Hu, effectively making their guest the host. With the late-night congee came ham, preserved eggs, meat floss, fermented bean curd with shrimp roe, radishes pickled in lees-flavoured sauce, and other preserved delicacies. Their bright colours under the crystal chandelier made them particularly appetizing. “I should like a little wine,” Hu said. “My muscles and joints have been aching these last two days.” Such aches called for tiger-bone and papaya liquor, a medicinal spirit made by Hu Qingyu Hall and famous throughout the country. Hu had little capacity for alcohol, so the Seventh Lady filled his stemmed glass only halfway.

“Seventh Sister,” he asked, holding his glass, “when are you coming to Hangzhou? Mother keeps thinking of you.” “I think of her too. I am afraid I cannot get away before the year's end, but I shall certainly come in spring.” “There is something I want to discuss with you both. Mother will be sixty-nine next year and seventy the year after. While Xiangyin is here, I want to celebrate both birthdays—the nine and the ten.” Hu's retainers and employees had long been discussing a splendid celebration for his mother's seventieth birthday. Now he intended to use Zuo Zongtang's prestige as Governor-General of Liangjiang to give her a grand celebration a year earlier as well. The Seventh Lady did not object to celebrating next year. But custom favoured celebrating an age ending in nine rather than the following round number; doing both seemed excessive. Still, it sprang from filial affection, and she did not wish to spoil the occasion. “Nine or ten, either is good, so long as the old lady is happy.”

“It is hard to establish a grand style of life, and hard to scale it back,” Hu said. “Foreign dealings have expanded these past few years, and foreigners have brought us many things, good and bad. Fewer people learn the good than the bad. If a man is bad to begin with, and then learns foreign tricks that we Chinese do not understand, there is no telling what he will do. He could sell you as a coolie to Gold Mountain before you even understood how you had reached a foreign country. Is that not frightening, Seventh Sister?” Not understanding his point, she murmured a noncommittal assent. “Someone came to me for help recently,” Hu continued. “He might simply have asked, but he had another approach. ‘Mr Hu,’ he said, ‘if you fail to do what you ought to do, people will talk. It is not worth it.’ I answered, ‘Loyalty and filial duty are the foundations of life. Beyond them, what must I do? So long as I fulfil the five human relationships, nobody has grounds to criticize my conduct.’ ‘Not so,’ he replied. ‘Beyond those five relationships, there is one thing that you, Mr Hu, ought to do.’ I asked what it was. What do you think he said? ‘Spend money.’” His argument was that Hu was famous for extravagant generosity, so any occasion requiring expenditure was properly his responsibility. Otherwise, he would cease to be Hu Xueyan. The man then asked to borrow five hundred taels, but could not say what he wanted them for.

“I knew perfectly well that he wanted to pay gambling debts. Had he told me honestly, such a small amount would not have mattered. Instead, he said, ‘You need not ask what I want it for, Mr Hu. Nobody needs a reason to borrow from you. Everyone knows how generous you have always been and how much money you have thrown away. If word gets out that you are questioning me over five hundred taels, people will think you insist on getting value for every coin and are unwilling to waste anything.’ Tell me, should I have been angry?” “Of course,” Gu replied. “It was outright blackmail. He meant that unless you lent him the money, he would spread malicious stories. Detestable!” “Utterly detestable! I thought: if I refuse, naturally he will say nothing good of me. But if I lend it, a man with such a spiteful tongue will take the benefit and sneer at me too. He will say, ‘Look, I called him a fool to his face, and he still did not dare refuse. He is like a candle that gives no light until someone strikes a match.’ What do you think I should have done?” “If it were me,” the Seventh Lady said indignantly, “I would give the five hundred—but he would never spend it. I would donate it to a charity in his name.” Hu sighed. “If only I had possessed your wit at the time, Seventh Sister.” “Why?” Gu asked. “What did you do wrong, Little Uncle?”

“I gave a cold laugh and said, ‘True, I have thrown away I do not know how much money in my life. But you are the one exception.’ I happened to have a thousand-tael note from Beijing's Four Great Heng banks in my pocket. ‘It seems I am destined to lose money today,’ I said. ‘There is no helping it.’ Then I struck a match and burned the note before his eyes.” “What did he do? Was he furious?” “He was not. He said something that made me furious.” “What?” “‘Do not try tricks for fooling children on me, Mr Hu. Fukang and the Four Great Heng are in the same business. You can report the burned note as lost.’” Gu and his wife fell silent. At last the Seventh Lady said, “Little Uncle, you suffered an injury you could not answer.” So he had. It had never occurred to Hu to register the note as lost. Once the man suggested it, however, he could no longer do so without proving the accusation that he had merely staged a children's trick. “Later, when people asked, I admitted the incident. If they asked whether I had reported the loss, I could only smile and say, ‘What do you think?’” “It is better when people ask,” Gu observed. “At least they can see your manner for themselves. The danger is those who hear the story and immediately assume you must have reported it, without thinking a question necessary. A'qi is right. You suffered badly from this.”

“One must learn from a loss,” Hu replied. “Afterwards I thought the fellow did have a point. Spending money is what I ought to do. I should never have asked his purpose. If my spending is wasteful, what about the money I earn? From my side, I earn through judgment, skill, energy, and effort. But I ought to consider the man who loses. If he regards his loss as money thrown away, then what I gain is that same thrown-away money.” “Your reasoning grows more mysterious all the time,” Gu said with a laugh. “Can earning money be a waste too?” “If you do not know how to use it, earning it is a waste. Have you heard of the ‘death-bell loans’ around Huai'an and Yangzhou?” Gu had never heard the expression, but the Seventh Lady knew it. Some rich merchants counted every penny, accumulated enormous fortunes, and yet ate and dressed miserably, clinging to each coin as though it were life itself. Unfortunately, they sometimes produced wastrel sons. With their fathers keeping such a tight grip on the purse, the sons borrowed wherever they could. Interest was even more savage than on the instalment loans of the Shanxi moneylenders. But there was one advantage: if the prodigal could not pay, the creditors would never press him. “When, then, did repayment fall due?” the Seventh Lady explained to Gu. “On the day his father died. As soon as the old man stopped breathing, the first thing was to summon a monk to chant the prayers at the deathbed. The moment the monk struck his chime, the creditors came to the door. That is why they were called death-bell loans.” “Better spend it oneself than leave it for unfilial descendants,” Gu said. “What one has gained oneself, one may lose oneself; that need not matter. But the proposition that every expense is your duty, Little Uncle—perhaps that still deserves some consideration.”

“I have thought it over repeatedly. Since people call me the God of Wealth, I ought to distribute wealth. Otherwise I invite trouble.” Hu abruptly returned to his original subject. “Take Mother's sixty-ninth birthday next year. I must celebrate it. If I do not, those who envy me will have something to say. They will say I have always loved appearances, and that with His Excellency Zuo now Governor-General of Liangjiang, I ought to be eager to borrow his prestige for a grand display. If I refrain, it cannot be because I do not want one; it must be because Zuo no longer treats me as before. Of course he would send Mother a birthday present, but only an ordinary one. He would do nothing special to enhance the occasion. Better for me, then, to recognize my position and keep quiet. Seventh Sister, would people not say that if I held no celebration?” She could not deny it, but answered differently. “There is nothing wrong with celebrating the sixty-ninth.” “And after celebrating it next year, I must celebrate again the year after. Otherwise people will say Mother's seventieth had long been planned, but I brought it forward a year to exploit Zuo's prestige. Having held it once, I let it suffice, because my circumstances have declined and I must economize where I can. You must understand, Seventh Sister, that this would be worse than not celebrating next year.” “Why?” “Do you not see?” Gu intervened. “Once that rumour spreads, Fukang's deposits will shrink.” “Shrink is hardly the word!” Hu quoted a literary saying: “Pull one hair and the whole body moves. A major storm would break immediately.”

The Seventh Lady could not picture precisely what such a storm would mean. But seeing an unusually apprehensive expression on his face, she could not keep back something she had long wished to say. “Little Uncle, I too must advise you to draw things in. My meaning differs a little from your mother's. She says you should reduce the display where possible, instead of expanding it further. I mean that you should stop businesses you need not conduct, and manage properly those you ought to keep.” Gu was the first to find this painfully offensive. “What do you mean? Does Little Uncle need you to criticize his business?” “Yingchun!” Hu laid a hand over Gu's on the table to stop him. “Seventh Sister is the only person still willing to tell me the truth. I want to hear it.” He nodded emphatically. Gu had noticed that Hu's temperament was no longer quite what it had been. He feared his wife's bluntness would offend him; even if Hu said nothing, the evening would be spoiled. Since Hu welcomed unwelcome truths, Gu had no reason to obstruct her, although he still gave her a glance urging tact. “I have kept some things inside for a long time, without an opportunity to say them,” she began. “Since you wish to listen, I shall speak plainly. I am not afraid of offending people. If even one or two of my remarks reach you, their resentment will be worth it.”

From this introduction Hu knew she meant to criticize the people he employed. This was a matter in which he took great interest and pride. He believed that his achievement—an establishment surpassing even the Yangzhou salt merchants at their height in the Qianlong and Jiaqing reigns—rested on his ability both to judge people and to use them. Naturally, discovering a person's strengths and faults required open observation and discreet inquiry. Yet when listening to judgments of character, he followed principles of his own. First he examined the critic: was that person open to criticism? Only then did he weigh the remarks, distinguishing what he ought to hear from what the speaker merely wanted him to believe. The Seventh Lady was among the very few people he felt he should admire. He wanted not only to hear her judgments but to ensure that she left nothing unsaid. He therefore encouraged her. “Nobody will resent you, Seventh Sister, because nobody will know what you tell me. Say whatever you have observed. Even if I am at fault, do not spare me. I shall be grateful for the truth, never angry with you.” His sincerity made her feel that criticizing particular employees would not adequately express her loyalty. She must go deeper, to the source of the faults.

“To be honest, Little Uncle, I respect you less than I did ten or more years ago. But my concern for you has increased, not diminished. Sometimes I think about your affairs until I cannot sleep all night.” Hu was visibly shaken. “We are friends who have endured hardship together, Seventh Sister. What I most admire is your courage and integrity. I know I am not as considerate of others in everything as I was ten or more years ago. Still, I have not treated people badly. My establishment is large, but the people I employ are capable, and everything is held firmly together, inside and out. I do not understand what worries you so much that you cannot sleep.” “What worries me is that a great tree catches the wind. You are a towering lampstand, Little Uncle. So many people borrow your light to find their way and move ahead quickly and safely. Yet you cannot illuminate yourself.” Hu found this use of the familiar saying particularly apt, and listened still more attentively. “Fortunately, you can see clearly. There are no outsiders here today. Tell me honestly: what faults must I change?” She hesitated. Her first thought was that his very belief in the competence of all his people and the security of his affairs needed changing. But that sounded like a wholesale condemnation and might provoke resistance. There was a practical difficulty too. If he asked whether he must replace everyone, where so many replacements could be found at once, and whether they would all be trustworthy, she could not answer. Gu partly understood her hesitation. Fearing that excessive criticism would merely unsettle Hu without practical benefit, he suggested, “A'qi, describe one or two small incidents. Little Uncle will draw his own conclusions.” “Very well.” She thought briefly. “I shall tell you of two occasions when others offended people on your behalf, without your knowledge, and the blame was entered against your name.”

The first concerned Hu's garden. After it was completed, he disliked the rockery and decided to rebuild it. Several specialists inspected it and produced plans, but none impressed him. Eventually he heard of an eminent master in Beijing, Ying Chong, a native of Henan. Early in the Xianfeng reign, Ying had been a retainer of Prince Yi, Zaiyuan. The Xinyou coup destroyed Zaiyuan's household and cost him his life. Having watched the great mansion rise and then collapse, Ying was deeply affected. He withdrew to the Western Hills, shut his door, taught his children, and ignored outside affairs. Generous gifts received during Zaiyuan's ascendancy meant that a few years of simple living would not leave him destitute. He had no wish to return to worldly employment. But Hu's humble entreaties and generous payment, reinforced by the persuasive Liu Bucai, who had been sent to invite him, eventually brought him to Hangzhou. Having inspected the existing rockery and several unused designs, Ying thought them reasonably good. Alteration would suffice; complete rebuilding was unnecessary. Hu disagreed and insisted on starting afresh. Ying privately thought this the consequence of having too much money. Yet he could not say so: such frankness before their acquaintance had deepened might lead Hu to think he lacked the imaginative resources to dare demolish and rebuild it.

Stung by the desire to prove himself, Ying shut himself away and did not come downstairs for a month, until he had completed a preliminary design. Even then he would not show it. Each day he walked with his staff among the Six Bridges and Three Tianzhu Temples, or explored the Northern and Southern Peaks in search of secluded and remarkable scenery. At night he spread out the plans by lamplight and revised them carefully. After three months the work was finally complete: seventeen drawings, one general plan and sixteen detailed sheets. Strange rocks, unusual ravines, and countless winding turns made a small space suggest an immense landscape. The result inspired delighted admiration. Overjoyed, Hu entertained him at a lavish banquet and asked him to supervise construction. Ying agreed. A rockery required exceptional stones. Hangzhou, the Southern Song capital, contained many famous gardens, including abandoned ones. Ying inspected them all, without finding much to satisfy him. One day he came to a ruined garden by Gongyuan West Bridge, said to have been the ancestral shrine of Zhao Wenhua, Yan Song's adopted son. A stone lying on its side there caught his attention. Three qualities defined a fine ornamental rock: slenderness, wrinkled texture, and openings through its body. Although half buried, the exposed portion possessed all three, and Ying judged that the hidden half must be equally fine.

As he examined it from every angle, an old man whose beard and eyebrows were completely white strolled over. He wore a short jacket and straw sandals and carried a spotted-bamboo pipe. His clothes were not those of a gentleman, but his bearing suggested a great official retired into seclusion. Ying greeted him respectfully. “May I ask your surname, sir?” “You are too kind. Zhao. And yours?” “Ying. Is anyone responsible for this abandoned garden, Mr Zhao?” “Certainly. I am.” “Ah! Forgive my ignorance.” Ying repeatedly clasped his hands in greeting. Returning the salute with his pipe raised, Zhao asked why he wanted the keeper. “I hoped to ask about this stone.” Zhao nodded, looked him over, and said, “You seem to share Mi the Eccentric's passion. Since you ask, I must tell you. The stone has a distinguished history: it came from Genyue in Daliang.” So it had belonged to Emperor Huizong's Genyue garden, carried all the way from Kaifeng six or seven centuries earlier. Its rarity was obvious. “Perhaps you have not yet discovered its finest feature.” Zhao turned and called, “Little Fourth, bring a drying pole!” In Hangzhou, a bamboo pole for hanging clothes was called a langgan. Little Fourth knew what it was wanted for. Without a word he inserted it into one end of the stone. Only then did Ying notice a bowl-sized hole running right through it. The pole easily emerged at the other end. “A true thread of sky!” Ying immediately imagined the stone incorporated into the rockery, with the midday sun shining through it into a cavern as a round shaft of light. What an exquisite scene that would make.

“Mr Zhao,” he asked directly, “could you bear to part with it?” Zhao studied him again. “Are you building a garden for yourself, or finding materials for someone else?” “To be frank, the God of Wealth, Hu, invited me to remodel his garden. If I obtain this remarkable stone, I shall have to revise my design again.” “So it is for him!” Zhao shook his head. “I will not commit that sin.” Ying was astonished. “What do you mean?” “Mr Hu is admirable in many ways and has done a great deal of good. Unfortunately, these past few years he has become proud, extravagant, indulgent, and idle, quite changing his nature. Those despicable flatterers under him have made him forget all limits. Diligence and thrift build a household; pride and extravagance ruin it. Consider this very stone. Had Emperor Huizong not built Genyue and imposed his flower-and-rock transport levies, how could the Jin armies have reached Bianliang? Since garden building is your profession, you must have worked for many wealthy and powerful families. How many of their owners have worthy descendants? As for Mr Hu, his establishment has grown too large to control. A true friend would urge him to withdraw while there is time. Anyone who continues encouraging his reckless expenditure will sooner or later feel the reproach of conscience.”

The speech left Ying sweating and deeply regretting his decision to emerge from retirement. Yet matters had gone too far for him to return his fee and withdraw his plans. He could only plead urgent business at home and firmly decline the supervision. Unable to detain him despite repeated entreaties, Hu asked him to recommend a replacement. Ying found it hard to refuse. The design also embodied much effort, and he feared seeing it ruined by an incompetent hand. Among Hu's retainers was Zeng Xiaosu, who knew something of the art and occasionally offered original ideas in conversation. Ying therefore said that Zeng could undertake the task. Hu always wanted to establish a man's abilities before employing him. He summoned Zeng, had him examine the drawings in Ying's presence, and asked how long construction would take. “With a great master here,” Zeng said, smiling, “how could I venture an opinion?” “Not at all!” Ying interjected, giving him a meaningful glance. “Please make an estimate, Brother Xiaosu.” Zeng understood that this profitable assignment was probably within reach. He concentrated on calculations for a while, then asked, “When would you like it finished, sir?”

“How about fifty days?” “Fifty days would require one hundred and twenty workers.” Zeng counted on his fingers. “There are four grottoes in the design: twenty craftsmen for each, leaving forty men to transport stone. Five days to pound the mortar, twenty for construction, ten allowed for alterations, and ten to complete the tops. If everything goes smoothly, forty-five days will suffice. You may arrange your grand banquet for fifty days from the start.” Hu neither agreed nor disagreed, but turned to Ying. “What do you think?” “The calculation is intelligent, but rather tight. Any slackening during construction, and fifty days will be insufficient.” “I have allowed five days' margin,” Zeng replied. “You may not realize, sir, that elsewhere I might hesitate to promise a fixed date because materials or labour could be short. Here, whatever workers, money, or materials are needed can be supplied. I am confident of finishing in fifty days.” “That is true.” Ying's approval was like the certification of examination officials. In the provincial examination years corresponding to Zi, Wu, Mao, and You, the court first appointed senior officials who had passed both higher examinations to test the eligible capital officials; only those who passed could be sent out as chief and deputy examiners. Ying had similarly certified Zeng's competence to supervise, and Hu consequently trusted him without reservation.

An auspicious day was chosen, and work began. The old rockery had already been demolished. On the cleared ground, one hundred and twenty craftsmen formed twelve circles and began pounding mortar. The steward, Hu Yunfu, had instructed them beforehand: “No calling out while you pound. The old lady dislikes the noise.” There was a special reason for this. The mortar, known in Hangzhou as niaojiang, used a particular kind of leaf which, soaked in water, produced a thick liquid resembling the wood-shaving infusion women used to dress their hair. This was added to lime and yellow clay before pounding. Several men stood in a circle around the mixture, each holding a waist-high T-shaped rammer. Its shaft was a piece of chestnut wood as thick as a rice bowl, with a rounded iron head at the bottom and a firmly fitted crosspiece two chi long at the top. At the leader's signal, the men stepped back, straightened, and swung their rammers upward. As the tools descended, they stepped forward and bent, driving the heads heavily into the lime and clay. Another worker continuously ladled on the thick leaf infusion. At first, white lime and yellow clay remained distinct; gradually they blended, and the longer the pounding continued, the tougher the mixture became. In Hangzhou, tomb builders packed it around coffins. Once dry, it became extraordinarily hard, virtually impervious to blades and weapons. The rarity of grave robbery there was attributed to this mortar. When a burial had to be moved, there was a separate method for breaking it: the tomb was opened, strong liquor poured over the mortar and ignited, and, after the liquor and flames were exhausted, the material became brittle enough to work with a hoe.

When the Ming founder built Nanjing's walls, he had charged Shen Wansan, the immensely wealthy man of the late Yuan, with construction. Massive stones were joined with boiled glutinous-rice paste, enabling the walls to endure for centuries. Niaojiang could perform a similar function. What mattered most was prolonged, even pounding, making the leader's signals indispensable. These were the familiar heave-ho cries of labour. Their rhythm, while expressing the workers' exertion, naturally directed the force and speed of each stroke, counted the blows, and regulated the length of their steps. As they worked, the men slowly moved round to their right, both to ensure even mixing and to measure the labour performed. Usually twelve to sixteen circuits were needed to bring the mortar to its full strength. Besides tomb building, it was used in rockeries, where only this material could firmly join the stones. But the distinctive pounding chant was often heard around burial grounds in spring and autumn, inevitably suggesting that another grave was being built nearby. Hu's elderly mother disliked hearing it; hence Hu Yunfu's order for silence. Without the chant, the workers were like soldiers deprived of commands. Their movements became disordered and slow. Eager to succeed, Zeng scolded and shouted at them. They dared not voice their anger at work, but talked bitterly as they left. Their complaint was not that Zeng lacked consideration, but that the Hu household was cruel.

Cruelty was indeed occurring, though Hu knew nothing of it. Whenever a great household undertook construction, contractors or foremen were apt to skimp on labour or materials. In building a rockery there was little scope to economize on the stone, but labour could be cheated. Because Zeng was shrewd, the contractors dared not inflate the headcount; instead they passed apprentices and assistants off as skilled craftsmen. The first two days went well, but by the third something was wrong. Racking his brains, Zeng devised a rule: no wages could be drawn in advance, and payment would be made at the end of each day. A specially built long bench more than eight chi high stood by the garden gate. For each group of twelve men, twelve wage packets were placed on it. Everyone had to reach for his own; nobody could pass a packet to someone else. Anyone whose arm did not reach received nothing for his day's work. Young apprentices left empty-handed and tearful, but short adults were equally helpless. Zeng proudly claimed credit for the arrangement: tall men had ample strength, he said, while even a strong short man had limited power. What use was a rockery builder without strength? This was the surest means of retaining the able and eliminating the unfit. Public opinion, however, became appalling. As the story spread, it was said that Hu abused his power by making men work without paying them. Some protested that a man famous for charity could never be so harsh. But witnesses were available, and even those wishing to defend him were silenced.

Another incident was still more outrageous. One year, early in winter, Hu held Buddhist rites for his late father's posthumous birthday and distributed food and clothing. Anyone willing to endure the embarrassment of accepting charity could queue for a blue cotton padded jacket and four white-flour steamed buns, each as large as a rice bowl. Hu had personally inspected the jackets and tasted the buns, taking every care. The charitable event should have gone well. Instead, people cursed him through clenched teeth. Again, the fault lay in his choice of subordinates and their reckless conduct. Some recipients, wanting a little extra, joined the queue a second time for another portion. A generous view would recognize that they had spent further time and effort to obtain it, rather than gained something for nothing. Even a strict response need have gone no further than a reprimand. But the organizers devised a novel system. After receiving a jacket and buns, each person encountered a group of daizhao, as barbers were also called, waiting at the exit with a razor in each man’s hand. A patch of hair was shaved off as proof that charity had already been received. Anyone unwilling to submit had to forgo the gifts. “Little Uncle,” the Seventh Lady said, still angry at the recollection, “imagine someone queuing before dawn and waiting until noon, without knowing of this rule. To refuse would mean all that hardship for nothing. To accept would leave a bald patch advertising that he wore charity clothes. What a choice! How could people help feeling bitter?”

Hu's face alternately flushed and paled. Despite the late-autumn weather, sweat dampened his back. “I knew nothing of this, Seventh Sister. When I return, I shall investigate and give the culprit a thorough dressing-down.” “There is no need. The man no longer works for you. That is why I have spoken.” “Then there are still others like him there?” She was silent, which amounted to assent. Since matters had reached this point, Gu decided to add his own counsel. He had followed Hu for years and knew much of the difficulty of establishing the business; his advice was therefore both extensive and penetrating. “You regard your pawnshops as a service to the poor, Little Uncle, and say you do not want to make money from them. But what pawnshop in the world makes no money? Because you have expressed that intention, even profits that ought properly to be earned are not appearing. Have you considered that?” “I have. I told them that a bank is a rich man's pawnshop, and a pawnshop is a poor man's bank. I deal with the rich. They pledge their credit or their connections; I can generally judge whether to accept the pledge and how much it is worth. There are too many poor people for me to look after personally, so I entrust them to the staff, who must act according to conscience. I have treated those Huizhou friends well. Surely they cannot be entirely without conscience.” Pawnshop appraisers came from Huizhou, hence his name for them. Gu realized from this speech that Hu knew nothing of the accumulated abuses in his own pawnshops. He also saw that his own observations could be of real use.

“Do you know how many pawnshops you own, Little Uncle?” Hu was taken aback. Scratching his head, he said, “There must be twenty?” “Count them,” the Seventh Lady urged. “Start with Hangzhou.” First came Gongji, the earliest shop Hu had established; then Guangshun and Tai'an, at Gongzhen Bridge outside Wulin Gate, the starting point of the canal, set up especially for the convenience of the grain-transport brotherhood. Across Hangzhou, Huzhou, Jiaxing, Haining, Jinhua, and Quzhou in Zhejiang, Suzhou and Zhenjiang in Jiangsu, and Hubei and Hunan, there were twenty-three in all. A pawnshop's operating capital was called its shelf capital. By convention it was stated in copper cash rather than silver, at one thousand cash to a tael: ten thousand taels thus became ten thousand strings of a thousand cash. Shops varied in size, with shelf capital ranging from fifty thousand to two hundred thousand such strings. At an average of one hundred thousand each, the twenty-three shops represented 2,300,000 taels. If their pledged goods were valued instead, the figure would at least double. “Let us put the total at four and a half million taels,” Gu said. “A return of one per cent is a low estimate for a business like this. That would mean forty-five thousand taels a month—more than one could spend. You could have me give up all my other work and concentrate on managing these twenty-three pawnshops.” Hu calculated: forty-five thousand a month meant 540,000 a year. Yet he could not remember annual pawnshop profits ever exceeding two hundred thousand. On that reasoning, the Huizhou friends were swallowing more than three hundred thousand taels a year.

“My monthly expenditure, including all entertaining, is only forty or fifty thousand taels. If the pawnshops were properly managed, I could put myself beyond defeat. Where do you think I should begin reforming them, Yingchun?” “Naturally, with an audit and inspection.” “One shop after another, or all together at a single order?” “All together, of course.” “Are you talking without thinking?” the Seventh Lady interrupted. “Where will you find enough people to inspect twenty-three shops at once? It is not merely checking accounts. The pledged goods on the shelves must be examined too, and outsiders cannot do that.” “Seventh Sister,” Hu stopped her, “if Yingchun proposes it, he must have a method.” “Exactly!” Gu answered with satisfaction. “My method is quick, thorough, and unlikely to offend anyone. Consider: if we inspect one shop after another, we naturally start with those we distrust, taking them by surprise. If faults appear, well and good. But if a shop proves entirely sound, its people will resent the suspicion, and it will be harder to obtain their best service afterwards.”

“Enough preliminaries!” the Seventh Lady said impatiently. “If you have a method, tell us.” “It leaves no sign of suspicion. Little Uncle, make a general reshuffle. Transfer all the managers and custodians of pledged goods among the twenty-three shops. Transfers require formal handovers, and each person taking over becomes responsible. Naturally, he will not dare be careless. In this way, both the accounts and the actual goods on the shelves will be thoroughly checked.” “That is ingenious. But moving a man from a small shop to a large one will cause no complaint; moving him from a large one to a small one certainly may.” “There is a remedy. Divide the shops into three classes according to size, and have those within each class draw lots for exchanges. The differences will be limited, and everyone will depend on his luck, leaving little ground for complaint.” “Besides,” the Seventh Lady added, “you can privately reassure and reward the few who are truly capable and have done well.” “Quite right. I shall arrange it when I return to Hangzhou.”
